name: Design a Food Delivery Platform
intent: Move an order safely through restaurant, courier and customer, pick which courier carries which orders, and promise an arrival time that holds even in the lunch rush.
codeTitle: an order state machine and a courier dispatcher
finalIntro: One lunch order, from the tap to the doorstep.
prompt: Design a food delivery platform for a large city. Customers browse restaurant menus and place an order, the restaurant accepts and cooks it, and a courier picks it up and delivers it. At the lunch peak, tens of thousands of orders arrive within an hour. Customers want an accurate arrival time and live tracking, and nobody should be charged for food that never arrives.
functional: Show restaurant menus, with items that can run out or be paused
Place an order and pay for it
Let the restaurant accept, prepare and mark the order, with cancellation while it is still allowed
Choose a courier for each order, and carry two orders at once where that helps
Show an arrival time and live tracking until delivery
nonFunctional: Every order follows legal state changes only, and no state change is lost or applied twice
The customer, the restaurant and the courier never disagree for long about what state an order is in
A courier assignment decision takes a few seconds at most, even at the peak
The promised arrival time is right within about five minutes for most orders
Handle a lunch peak of several times the average load without dropping orders
Never charge for an order that is cancelled, and never lose a paid order
Keep food hot: little time between the food being ready and the courier leaving with it

firstAttempt.text: One server and one database. An orders table has a status column that every app overwrites. The restaurant tablet sets the status to accepted, the courier app sets picked up and delivered, and the customer cancel button sets cancelled. When an order is placed, the server looks for the nearest free courier and sends the order to them straight away. The arrival time is a fixed 30 minutes.
limits: Anyone can write any status, so an order can go from delivered back to preparing, or be cancelled after the food is on the way
Two apps writing at the same time overwrite each other, so a cancel and an accept can both appear to succeed
Nearest-first sends a courier the moment the order is placed, and the courier then stands at the counter for ten minutes while the food is cooked
Choosing couriers one order at a time never sees the better pairing, so one courier takes a long detour while another idles nearby
A fixed 30 minutes is wrong for most orders, and a busy kitchen or a long trip makes it badly wrong
Every menu view, location ping and status read hits the same database, so the lunch peak brings everything down at once

steps.title: Make the order a state machine with one owner
steps.problem: When every app can write any status, orders end up in impossible states, and two people acting at the same moment can both think they won.
steps.fix: An order service is the only writer. An order is always in one of these states: placed, accepted, preparing, picked up, delivered or cancelled. A table lists the legal moves, such as placed to accepted and preparing to picked up, and each move has an owner. The restaurant moves it to accepted and preparing, the courier moves it to picked up and delivered, and the customer or a timeout can move it to cancelled, but only before pickup, and once cooking has started a cancel is a request that the service may refuse. Every request names the state it expects and carries a version number, and the database applies it only if the version still matches, so two competing changes cannot both succeed. Each accepted change is appended to an event log together with the new state, so the history of an order is never lost.
steps.tradeoff: Illegal and conflicting changes are impossible, and a dispute can be settled by reading the log. The price is that some taps are refused, so the apps must handle a 'too late, the food is already on its way' answer, and all writes to one order go through one place.

steps.title: Serve menus and availability from their own fast store
steps.problem: Menus are read about twenty times for every order placed, and an item that sold out must stop being offered quickly, or the restaurant has to refuse an order the customer has already paid for.
steps.fix: A menu service owns menus, prices, opening hours and stock, and the apps read it through a cache. The restaurant can pause an item, mark it sold out or pause the whole kitchen with one tap, and the change is pushed into the cache rather than waiting for it to expire. When the order is placed, the order service checks the items against the current menu and stores a copy of the names and prices in the order, so later menu edits never change an existing order. If an item is gone at that moment, the customer is told before paying.
steps.tradeoff: Browsing is fast and cheap, and an order always has a stable price. The menu a customer sees can be a few seconds stale, so the final check at placement is what really decides, and a tablet that is offline cannot update availability.

steps.title: Publish state changes as events, and start dispatch from them
steps.problem: Dispatch, ETA, payments and notifications all need to react to an order change, and the order service must not be slowed by any of them or lose a change when one of them is down.
steps.fix: The order service writes the new state and an 'outbox' record in the same database transaction, and a relay then publishes the record to an event bus. The dispatcher, the ETA (estimated time of arrival) service, payments and notifications each read the bus at their own pace. The dispatcher starts looking for a courier when it sees an order accepted, and an event carries the order id and version so a consumer that sees it twice does the work only once.
steps.tradeoff: The services are decoupled, and a slow consumer cannot hold up an order. Everything downstream now runs a moment behind the truth, and consumers must tolerate repeated and out-of-order events by checking the version.

steps.title: Dispatch in batches and assign globally, not nearest-first
steps.problem: Sending the nearest free courier the instant each order arrives wastes couriers: they stand at the counter while the food is cooked, one courier takes a far trip that another could do on the way, and no courier ever carries two orders.
steps.fix: The dispatcher collects orders for a short window, from a few seconds up to a minute or two, and then decides all of them together. It builds a table of the cost of every courier for every order that is due, where the cost adds the time the food will wait for the courier, the time the courier will wait for the food, and the distance, and it solves the assignment problem for the whole table (finding the cheapest pairing of couriers to orders), with a method such as the Hungarian algorithm. Orders are due when the time left until the food is ready is about the courier's travel time, so the courier arrives as the food does. Orders from nearby restaurants to nearby customers can be paired onto one courier when the detour is small. Couriers who are about to finish a delivery can be assigned too. Dispatchers are partitioned by city zone, so each decision involves hundreds of couriers rather than the whole country.
steps.tradeoff: Couriers wait less, food is fresher and fewer couriers handle more orders, especially when couriers are scarce. A short window delays each decision slightly, pairing makes the first order of a pair wait for the second pickup, and the solver and its cost weights need tuning and monitoring.

steps.title: Estimate the arrival time from its parts, and keep updating it
steps.problem: A fixed promise is wrong for most orders, and an arrival time that is wrong in the optimistic direction makes customers cancel or complain.
steps.fix: The ETA service adds up the parts. The kitchen time comes from that restaurant's recent prep times for this kind of order, plus its current queue of open orders. The courier's travel to the restaurant and from the restaurant to the customer come from a routing model with live speeds. Parking and hand-over time are added, and the pickup time is the later of the courier arriving and the food being ready. The result is shown as a range, and it is recomputed when the order changes state, when the courier moves or when the kitchen reports delay. A tracking gateway holds a connection to each watching app and pushes the new time and the courier position, in batches, rather than being polled.
steps.tradeoff: Customers see an honest and moving estimate, and the estimate error can be measured against what really happened. Every part has its own error, a very busy kitchen is hard to predict, and showing a range or padding the promise trades a longer number against fewer broken promises.

steps.title: Shape the lunch peak instead of only absorbing it
steps.problem: Within one hour at noon, load is several times the average, kitchens fall behind, couriers run out and every number in the system gets worse together.
steps.fix: Peak controls watch each restaurant's queue and each zone's courier supply. When a kitchen is behind, it quotes a longer prep time, stops taking new orders for a few minutes, or limits how many open orders it will accept. When couriers are scarce, the dispatcher widens its window and allows more pairing, and a pay boost brings couriers into the zone. Customers see a longer, honest estimate, or can choose to schedule for later. Rate limits protect the order API, and everything that is not on the order's critical path, such as recommendations, is switched off first.
steps.tradeoff: The platform degrades in a controlled way, with slower and honest orders instead of dropped ones. Some customers see a closed restaurant or a longer estimate at the busiest time, and the rules need tuning so that they do not swing back and forth.

failures.scenario: The restaurant tablet goes offline after an order is placed
failures.impact: The order sits in placed, the customer has paid, and nobody is cooking.
failures.answer: An order must be accepted within a short deadline, such as two minutes, and a timer on the order service moves it to cancelled when the deadline passes, which voids the payment authorisation. The tablet sends a heartbeat (a regular "I am alive" signal), so a kitchen that has gone quiet is paused in the menu before it receives more orders, and a phone call or text is tried before the cancel.

failures.scenario: The customer cancels at the same moment the restaurant accepts
failures.impact: Both apps show success, and the kitchen cooks food that is owed a refund, or the customer is charged for an order they cancelled.
failures.answer: Both requests name the state they expect, and the database accepts only the first one that matches the current version. The other gets a clear refusal and its app refreshes. After preparing starts, a cancel is no longer a plain state change: it is a request that the order service may refuse, or accept with a partial charge.

failures.scenario: A courier goes silent or abandons the order after pickup
failures.impact: The food is cooling, the customer's estimate keeps growing and nobody is responsible.
failures.answer: The courier app reports its position every few seconds, and a missing heartbeat or a stalled position raises a case. Before pickup the dispatcher simply reassigns the order. After pickup the order stays picked up, support is alerted, and a replacement meal or a refund is decided by a person or a rule, with the event log showing what happened.

failures.scenario: A state change is delivered twice, or arrives out of order
failures.impact: A delivered tap sent twice could trigger two payouts, and an old 'preparing' event processed after 'picked up' could move the order backwards.
failures.answer: Each change carries a unique request id and the version it expects, so a repeat returns the earlier result and is not applied again. Consumers of the bus compare the event's version with what they already hold and ignore anything older. Payments and payouts use the order id as an idempotency key.

failures.scenario: A lunch rush: orders triple and a third of the couriers are busy
failures.impact: Cooked food waits on the counter, estimates slip and the dispatcher cannot find a courier for the oldest orders.
failures.answer: The peak controls lengthen quoted prep times and pause the busiest kitchens, the dispatcher allows more two-order trips so each courier carries more, and a pay boost draws couriers into the zone. If supply still falls short, orders wait in the dispatcher's queue with an honest, longer estimate, and the oldest are served first.

alternatives.title: How couriers are chosen

options.name: Nearest free courier, at once
options.pro: Trivial to build and fast to decide
options.con: Couriers wait at the counter, and local choices block better global ones

options.name: Batching two orders per courier
options.pro: Far fewer couriers needed when supply is tight
options.con: The first order of a pair waits, so it can make food colder or later

options.name: Window-based global assignment
options.pro: Matches couriers to orders by the cost of waiting on both sides
options.con: A short decision delay and a solver that needs tuning

alternatives.pick: A short window with global assignment as the base, adding pairing when couriers are scarce. Nearest-first remains the fallback if the solver is slow.

alternatives.title: When a courier is sent

options.name: As soon as the order is accepted
options.pro: The simplest, and the shortest wait for a courier to be found
options.con: The courier often arrives long before the food

options.name: At about ready time minus travel time
options.pro: The courier arrives as the food does, so neither waits
options.con: Needs a good prep estimate, and a late kitchen leaves the courier with an idle gap

alternatives.pick: Dispatch at ready time minus travel, with the estimate adjusted by each kitchen's recent accuracy.

alternatives.title: How the order state is stored

options.name: A status column with a version number
options.pro: Simple, and the compare-and-set update makes races safe
options.con: History is lost unless it is written elsewhere

options.name: An append-only event log with a current-state row
options.pro: Full history for disputes, and events feed the other services
options.con: More to build, and the two must be written together

alternatives.pick: A current-state row with its version, plus an event log written in the same transaction.

alternatives.title: How the apps learn about changes

options.name: Polling every few seconds
options.pro: Works everywhere and is easy to scale
options.con: Mostly empty requests, and a delay of a poll interval

options.name: A held connection with pushed updates
options.pro: Instant updates and less wasted traffic
options.con: Connections to manage, and a fallback is needed when they drop

alternatives.pick: Push for customers who are watching an order, with polling as the fallback. Restaurants also get a push, as their tablets must never miss an order.

roles.description: Order events on their way to the services that react.

quiz.question: A customer taps Cancel in the same second a restaurant taps Accept. Today every app writes the status column directly, so both appear to succeed and the kitchen starts cooking an order that is owed a refund. What is the right design?
options: Each app sends its own device timestamp with the tap, and the order service applies the change with the earlier timestamp, because the tap that came first should win.
Add a separate 'cancelled' flag that is set independently of the status, and let the kitchen check the flag before cooking.
Lock the order row while the restaurant tablet shows the order, so the customer cannot cancel until the restaurant decides.
The order service is the only writer; each request names the version it saw, and the database applies only the first match while the other gets a refusal.
quiz.explanation: A compare-and-set on a version lets exactly one of two competing changes win, and the loser is told to refresh. Device clocks are not trustworthy enough to order two taps. A separate flag recreates the conflict in two places, and a lock held while a person decides can block the order for minutes.

quiz.question: A restaurant says the food will be ready 14 minutes after it accepts, and the nearest free courier is 6 minutes away from the restaurant. The goal is that neither the courier nor the food waits. When should the courier be sent?
options: 8 minutes after acceptance, so the courier reaches the counter just as the food comes out.
Immediately on acceptance, for the shortest search time.
11 minutes after acceptance, halfway between sending at once and sending at ready time.
14 minutes after acceptance, when the food is ready, so the courier never arrives early.
quiz.explanation: Sent at 8 minutes, the courier arrives at 14, exactly as the food is ready. Sent immediately, the courier arrives at 6 and stands at the counter for 8 minutes. Sent at 11, the courier arrives at 17 and the food sits cooling for 3 minutes. Sent at 14, the courier arrives at 20 and the food sits cooling for 6 minutes. The estimate must be adjusted by how accurate that kitchen has been.

quiz.question: At the lunch peak, orders triple, a third of couriers are busy, and several kitchens are falling behind. Which response keeps orders honest and avoids dropping them?
options: Assign the nearest free courier the instant each order arrives, to keep decision time as low as possible.
Keep the 30-minute promise and cancel automatically any order that the system can already see will be late.
Quote longer prep times and pause new orders at the busiest kitchens, allow more two-order trips, and raise courier pay in the zone.
Close ordering for the whole city once couriers run short and reopen it after the peak has passed.
quiz.explanation: Load is shaped, not only absorbed: kitchens and the dispatcher slow the inflow and use scarce couriers better, and customers see a longer but true estimate. Nearest-first wastes couriers at the counter. Cancelling late orders or closing the city drops orders that could have been served.
